subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 49-year-old woman with central obesity and hypertriglyceridemia is found to have hepatic steatosis on ultrasound. Laboratory studies show fasting triglycerides of 310 mg/dL and normal aminotransferases. After a high-carbohydrate meal, her liver increases citrate export from mitochondria to the cytosol and synthesizes fatty acids.
question: Which of the following best describes the role of citrate in this process?

options.text: It is converted directly to acetyl-CoA by citrate synthase
It activates hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue
It inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase, limiting fatty acid synthesis
It allosterically activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, promoting fatty acid synthesis

explanation_correct: Citrate is transported from the mitochondrial matrix to the cytosol, where it is cleaved by ATP citrate lyase to acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate and allosterically activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase. The resulting malonyl-CoA is used for fatty acid synthesis, which contributes to hepatic steatosis after carbohydrate-rich meals.

explanation_incorrect.A: Citrate does inhibit phosphofructokinase-1, but this is not the mechanism by which it promotes fatty acid synthesis after a carbohydrate load.
explanation_incorrect.B: Citrate synthase catalyzes the opposite direction, forming citrate from oxaloacetate and acetyl-CoA; in the cytosol citrate is cleaved to acetyl-CoA by ATP citrate lyase.
explanation_incorrect.C: Citrate does not activate hormone-sensitive lipase; insulin and catecholamines regulate lipolysis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Citrate activates, rather than inhibits, acetyl-CoA carboxylase.

educationalObjective: TCA-derived citrate is exported to the cytosol, where it supplies acetyl-CoA and allosterically activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase for fatty acid synthesis.
